Can mathematical reasoning be given foundations whose reliability can itself be established?

The notion of computability finds its origin in establishing the reliability of mathematical reasoning. The purpose of mathematics is to provide objective grounds for establishing truth through the following scheme: choose your domain and fix your axioms and rules of inference. Now, everything related to the domain must be settled by starting with the axioms and following the rules.
What must a computation remember in order to undo what it has done?
An AND gate that outputs 0 cannot say which of three inputs it received. Computing without such losses requires keeping more than the answer.
How can two steps that each look random combine into a certain result?
A quantum step can look as random as a coin flip, yet two such steps in a row can give a certain result. Explaining how leads to the central ideas of quantum mechanics.

Different orthonormal bases give different measurement procedures. Their inner products determine outcome probabilities, while eigenspaces attach numerical values to outcomes. The same inner products also limit how well a measurement can distinguish two preparations.
Can a whole have a definite quantum state when its parts have no individual pure states of their own?
Two qubits can have a pure joint state while neither has an individual pure-state vector. We will calculate what this changes about copying, communication, and measurement.
Can we learn a relation among answers without learning the individual answers themselves?
One quantum query can reveal whether \(f(0)\) equals \(f(1)\), although no measurement reveals either value.
What separates an operation we can describe mathematically from one we can construct with finite means?
Every quantum operation can be built from a few kinds of gate, but not every operation can be built cheaply.
How can a process concentrate our chances of finding an answer that it can recognize but does not yet know?
Marking an answer with a sign does not change its probability. Repeated reflection turns the sign into a rotation toward the answer.
What would justify saying that one form of computation is more powerful than another?
A faster algorithm shows what is possible; only a lower bound shows what is impossible. Establishing an advantage needs both.
